title: Qualcomm's $5 billion data-center chip ramp is now an execution test, not a strategy question
subtitle: Management targets $5 billion in fiscal 2027 data-center revenue with a $7 billion annual run rate by year end, two hyperscaler customers carrying most of that mix, and Morningstar raising fair value even as it says Nvidia's moat is not threatened.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Qualcomm's data-center AI business, dormant for years and reintroduced at its June investor event, is now a concrete short-term ramp. CFO Akash Palkhiwala guided fiscal 2027 data-center revenue to $5 billion, with about $1 billion of that from the new custom-chip customers. The November 4 earnings report tightened the first quarter to above $650 million, with revenue growing each quarter and exiting fiscal 2027 at a $7 billion annual run rate. By fiscal 2029, management has publicly projected $15 billion in annual data-center chip sales.

The structural detail investors are watching is customer concentration. Two hyperscaler customers are expected to account for most fiscal 2027 data-center revenue, with Microsoft and Meta named in product briefings as users of Qualcomm's new AI chips. That concentration is also an execution risk: a design win delay, a workload rebalance, or an architecture change at either customer can move the top-line number by a lot. The business is also margin-dilutive while it ramps — the company guided QCT EBT margin in the 20–22 percent range for the first quarter, with the data-center investment costing about three percentage points.

The context is shifting. Morningstar raised its fair value estimate on Qualcomm to $200 from $155, calling the data-center forecast better than expected, but added that it does not anticipate Qualcomm usurping Nvidia's wide moat or early-mover advantage. Bank of America had previously modeled a wider $2 billion to $5 billion range by fiscal 2027–2028. The new specificity moves Qualcomm into a different story — no longer whether it can enter the AI data-center market at all, but whether it can hit its stated numbers while Nvidia's own supply, legal and geopolitical issues dominate the headlines.

A note for learners: when a semiconductor company commits to a dollar number for a new business line, the first question is customer-count. One or two customers makes it a bet on those specific hyperscalers' roadmaps; a diversified customer book makes it a bet on the chip. Qualcomm's $5 billion is the former. That is not a problem so long as the named customers scale their workloads, but it is a different kind of risk than a broad merchant-silicon business like Nvidia's — and the right valuation framework is different too.
